key_concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation $eV_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}$: emission needs $\lambda < \lambda_0$, and a larger threshold wavelength (smaller work function) gives a larger stopping potential.
steps: Write Einstein's equation in terms of wavelengths: $eV = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = hc\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)$. Emission occurs only if $\lambda < \lambda_0$, i.e. the incident photon energy exceeds the work function.
Cell 1: $\lambda_1 < \lambda$, so the photon energy $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ is less than the work function $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1}$. No photoelectrons are emitted, so $V_1 = 0$.
Cell 2: $\lambda_2 > \lambda$, so emission occurs and $eV_2 = hc\left(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_2}\right) > 0$.
Cell 3: $\lambda_3 \gg \lambda$, so $\dfrac{1}{\lambda_3} \approx 0$ and $eV_3 \approx \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. This is the maximum possible value, since the work function is nearly zero.
The condition $\lambda_3 \gg \lambda$ implies $\lambda_3 > \lambda_2$, so $\dfrac{1}{\lambda_3} < \dfrac{1}{\lambda_2}$. Subtracting less from the same $\dfrac{1}{\lambda}$ gives $V_3 > V_2$.
why_not_others: Options (3) and (4) wrongly put $V_3 = 0$, when cell 3 has the largest threshold wavelength and so emits most easily. Option (2) reverses the order: a larger $\lambda_0$ means a smaller work function and therefore a larger stopping potential, not a smaller one.
common_trap: Students treat threshold wavelength like threshold frequency and think a larger $\lambda_0$ means a larger work function, which reverses the order of $V_2$ and $V_3$.
time_saving_tip: Remember: emission happens only if $\lambda < \lambda_0$, and the bigger $\lambda_0$ is, the bigger $V_0$ is. Cell 1 fails, so $V_1 = 0$; cell 3 has the biggest threshold, so it has the biggest stopping potential.
